verdict.reasoning: Patient reports anxiety, palpitations and poor sleep over about two months: "I've been feeling really anxious over the past few months"; palpitations "only in the past... couple of months"; sleep: "maybe, three, four hours, I'm getting now."

She links onset to a new, stressful fashion retail head office job: "maybe about two months or so... and that probably coincides with, me starting a new job" and "I work for a... fashion retailer, in... the head office team... it's been really stressful."

She states bedtime and short sleep duration with long latency: "About ten, eleven, probably" and "Not for ages, I'm, I'm lying awake all night" and estimates "maybe, three, four hours, I'm getting now."

Palpitations details match: she says it feels irregular ("Irregular, I think"), lasts "couple of minutes" up to "like ten minutes," mainly around waking in the morning, and denies classic chest pain: "Any chest pain with that?" – "No, um, well yeah it's painful... when my heart is beating fast but..." indicating no separate true chest pain.

She describes daytime fatigue, anhedonia, and avoiding friends/exercise: "It's just, really, really low... I find no enjoyment at all"; "anything that, previously was, really fun is just not... enjoyable"; "I avoid them" regarding friends; and reduced exercise: "I did used to... go running... and to play tennis... but now... I'm not going out to do that quite so much."

Her mood is low but she denies suicidal thoughts: "I'm pretty much, down" and "I haven't had any suicidal thoughts or any, thoughts that have been that extreme... I don't have, uh worries about, actually wanting to, um, not go on."

She reports stable appetite with more chocolate: "Probably, not, significant changes maybe... No I wouldn't say that I'm eating like, much differently. Ohh that, I probably have more chocolate than normal, just because I feel, so down."
She describes her mother’s history: "I talk to my mum, because she also suffers from, well she's, suffered from like depression in the past."
She lives with parents and describes good support: "I live with my parents, just my parents" and "I have a good support system, like I do have good family and stuff."
Alcohol pattern matches: "probably quite a lot on the Friday or Saturday" and "I probably go over my limit just on those days" plus weekday wine: "maybe a glass of wine during the week."
She is an occasional smoker and denies drugs: "I try not to smoke, but I do, occasionally, but I don't take drugs."
She agrees to one-to-one therapy: when asked "would you be happy to, have, some one-to-one therapy?" she replies, "Yeah I think, yeah I think so... yeah."

Her anxiety is clearly work-focused and associated with insomnia and impact on functioning: she dreads work and feels very stressed at work; describes severe sleep disturbance; and notes functional impairment: "It's really impacting on... the rest of my life" and loss of enjoyment and reduced activities.

Doctor states palpitations are probably anxiety-related but will investigate: "it is most likely to be... associated with anxiety, but it's probably worth having couple of basic blood tests just to make sure that, there's not something triggering that off."
Low mood without suicidality is documented: she is "pretty much, down" and explicitly says "I haven't had any suicidal thoughts."

Doctor proposes IAPT-style talking therapy: "you can self-refer via the NHS, for what we call like, talking therapy..." and "I can send you the link for that." (Equivalent to IAPT self-referral for CBT/talking therapy.)

Doctor plans online anxiety/sleep resources: "There are some online resources that are really helpful. Um, can put the details, on there and you can, get on with them straight away" and "I'll put some more information on your notes about, helping with your, sleep patterns and things like that."

Basic blood tests and booking via support line are arranged: "it's probably worth having couple of basic blood tests" and "So if you call the support line you can arrange the, to have the blood test done."
A GP review one week after tests is planned: "then arranging a GP follow-up a week after you've had the tests, so we can just go through the results with you."

Safety advice to call sooner if worsening: "if you're feeling like it's not helping at all, or your anxiety is getting worse, to the point where you can't cope with work, or you can't, just do your normal things day-to-day. Then, it's important for us to, for you to give us a call, back and just discuss that, further."
Doctor comments on her visible distress: "I mean, I can see that you're quite distressed by like that." This supports that she appeared distressed during the consult.
